# Building a Principal-Level Kubernetes SRE Teammate: n8n, Groq Llama 3.3 70B, and 20 Custom Kubectl Tools **Author:** [Anshul Bisht](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht) **Date:** June 2026 **Category:** Kubernetes / SRE / Agentic Automation **Reading Time:** 10 min **Repository:** [github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Kubernetes-Agent-Teamate](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Kubernetes-Agent-Teamate) --- ## Executive Summary Navigating a complex Kubernetes cluster during an operational incident often feels like playing 20 questions with the command line: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl describe pod`, `kubectl logs`, `kubectl get events`, `kubectl top nodes`. SREs spend valuable minutes gathering scattered cluster context before they can even begin reasoning about the root cause. **AI Kubernetes Agent Teammate** is a self-hosted, conversational Site Reliability Engineering assistant. Powered by **n8n**, **Groq's ultra-low-latency LPU inference** (`llama-3.3-70b-versatile`), and a custom containerized environment equipped with **20 dedicated `kubectl` tools**, this agent acts as an autonomous virtual teammate. It answers natural-language questions about your cluster, gathers deep contextual evidence across namespaces, diagnoses bottlenecks, and executes verified remediation actions—all accessible via a web chat HUD or your mobile phone via **Telegram**. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Users["Operator Interfaces"] WebChat["n8n Web Chat Interface"] TelegramUser["Telegram Mobile App"] end subgraph Orchestrator["Containerized SRE Hub (n8n v1.123)"] Agent["LangChain Conversational Agent"] Groq["Groq LPU Engine
(Llama 3.3 70B Versatile)"] Memory["Conversation Window Buffer"] subgraph ToolSuite["20 Autonomous Kubectl Tools"] direction TB subgraph ReadTools["13 Read Tools"] R1["get_pods · get_nodes"] R2["describe_pod · get_logs"] R3["get_events · top_nodes · top_pods"] end subgraph WriteTools["7 Write Tools (Gated ⚠️)"] W1["scale_deployment · restart_deployment"] W2["patch_resource · rollout_undo"] W3["apply_manifest · delete_resource · exec_in_pod"] end end end subgraph Cluster["Kubernetes Infrastructure"] K8sAPI["Kubernetes API Server
(Local kind / Remote AWS EKS)"] Workloads["Cluster Workloads
(Pods, Nodes, Deployments, Events)"] end WebChat & TelegramUser --> Agent Agent <--> Groq Agent --> Memory Agent --> ToolSuite ToolSuite -->|kubectl CLI calls| K8sAPI K8sAPI <--> Workloads ``` --- ## Why a Conversational Agent for Kubernetes? The goal of this system is not to replace human judgment, but to eliminate operational friction: - **Instant Context Aggregation:** Instead of typing five separate commands to investigate why a deployment failed, an engineer can simply ask: *"Why is the checkout pod crashing in the staging namespace?"* The agent autonomously describes the pod, fetches the last 100 log lines, checks recent cluster events, and summarizes the exact reason (e.g., an invalid Redis password secret). - **Mobile Triage on the Go:** By routing interactions through Telegram via Cloudflare Tunnels, an on-call engineer can triage and remediate cluster alerts directly from their phone while away from their workstation. - **Fast Reasoning with Groq:** By leveraging Groq's Language Processing Units (LPUs), inference speeds exceed 250 tokens per second, making multi-tool investigations feel instantaneous. --- ## The 20-Tool Kubernetes Operational Arsenal The agent is equipped with 20 distinct tools implemented as dedicated n8n workflows that wrap the `kubectl` binary inside the container. Tools are strictly categorized into **Read** operations and **Write (Mutating)** operations: ### 1. Read Operations (13 Tools) These tools collect cluster context autonomously without risk of modifying cluster state: | Tool Name | Scope | Description | |---|---|---| | `get_pods` | Cluster / NS | Lists pods, statuses, restart counts, and IP addresses. | | `get_nodes` | Cluster | Returns node statuses, roles, versions, and kernel details. | | `describe_pod` | Pod-level | Comprehensive pod specification, container states, and associated events. | | `describe_resource` | Generic | Deep inspection of Services, Ingresses, ConfigMaps, or PersistentVolumeClaims. | | `get_logs` | Container | Retrieves the last 100 log lines, handling multi-container pods. | | `get_deployments` | Cluster / NS | Lists deployment replica status (desired, updated, available). | | `get_services` | Cluster / NS | Inspects cluster IP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer configurations. | | `get_namespaces` | Cluster | Audits all active namespaces. | | `get_events` | Cluster / NS | Chronological event stream for error correlation (newest first). | | `get_ingresses` | Namespace | Inspects host rules, paths, and backend service bindings. | | `get_configmaps_secrets`| Namespace | Audits existing configuration objects and secret keys. | | `top_nodes` | Cluster | Real-time CPU and memory utilization across worker nodes. | | `top_pods` | Namespace | Real-time CPU and memory metrics per container. | --- ### 2. Write / Mutating Operations (7 Gated Tools ⚠️) These tools allow the agent to remediate issues, apply fixes, and execute operational commands: | Tool Name | Risk Level | Action Executed | |---|---|---| | `scale_deployment` | Medium | Dynamically adjusts replica counts (`kubectl scale deployment --replicas=N`). | | `restart_deployment` | Medium | Triggers a rolling restart (`kubectl rollout restart deployment `). | | `rollout_undo` | High | Rolls back a deployment to its previous stable revision. | | `patch_resource` | High | Applies a JSON Strategic Merge Patch to any Kubernetes manifest. | | `apply_manifest` | High | Applies a raw YAML manifest to the cluster. | | `delete_resource` | Critical | Permanently deletes a specified Kubernetes resource. | | `exec_in_pod` | High | Executes a non-interactive diagnostic command inside a running container. | --- ## Safety Architecture: The Explicit Confirmation Gate Allowing an LLM to invoke `kubectl delete` or `kubectl patch` without human verification is unacceptable in enterprise environments. The agent's system prompt enforces a mandatory **Safety Gate**: > **Strict Operational Rule:** Whenever a user request requires a Write or Mutating tool (`scale`, `restart`, `patch`, `delete`, `apply`, `exec`), you MUST NOT execute the tool immediately. You must present the exact planned command, explain the operational blast radius, and ask: *"Do you confirm this action? Please reply with 'yes' to proceed."* Only upon receiving explicit human confirmation may the write tool be called. This ensures that the agent handles the tedious diagnostics, but human operators maintain ultimate operational authority over cluster modifications. --- ## Solving the Docker Loopback & macOS Networking Puzzle Running a Dockerized agent that needs to talk to a local Kubernetes cluster (like `kind` or Docker Desktop Kubernetes) exposes a classic container networking issue: ### The Problem: Your `~/.kube/config` points to `server: https://127.0.0.1:6443`. When this kubeconfig is mounted into the n8n Docker container, `127.0.0.1` refers to the container's own internal loopback interface—not your host machine where the Kubernetes API server is actually listening. ### The Engineering Solution: 1. **Host Gateway Mapping:** We duplicate the kubeconfig into `./internal-kubeconfig.yaml` and update the server address: ```yaml server: https://host.docker.internal:6443 ``` 2. **TLS Verification Bypass for Local Containers:** Because the Kubernetes API server certificate is issued for `kubernetes` and `localhost` (not `host.docker.internal`), the connection would fail TLS validation. We configure: ```bash kubectl config set-cluster kind-cluster --insecure-skip-tls-verify=true ``` 3. **Container Mount:** We mount `./internal-kubeconfig.yaml` read-only into `/home/node/.kube/config` inside the container. The agent can now communicate seamlessly with local clusters. --- ## Telegram Sanitization & Formatting Resilience When operating via Telegram, raw Kubernetes command output often breaks the Telegram Bot API: - Telegram enforces a strict **4,096-character limit** per message. - Unescaped characters (like `<`, `>`, `_`, and `*` common in log outputs) trigger fatal `Bad Request: can't parse entities` errors in Telegram's Markdown parser. The workflow includes a dedicated JavaScript **Sanitizer Node** placed before the Telegram Sender: - Detects outputs exceeding 4,000 characters and intelligently splits them into sequential numbered turns. - Automatically strips or escapes unclosed markdown delimiters, ensuring 100% webhook delivery success. --- ## Quickstart: Deploying Your SRE Agent ### 1. Configure Environment ```bash git clone https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Kubernetes-Agent-Teamate.git cd AI-Kubernetes-Agent-Teamate cp .env.example .env # Set N8N_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD, GROQ_API_KEY, and TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN ``` ### 2. Launch Stack ```bash # Builds custom image with n8n + kubectl baked in docker compose up -d --build ``` ### 3. Expose for Telegram (Optional) ```bash cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:5678 # Copy the trycloudflare.com URL into .env as WEBHOOK_URL and restart ``` ### 4. Activate Tools 1. Open `http://localhost:5678`. 2. Import the tool workflows from `workflows/` and activate each one. 3. Import `workflows/k8s-agent-workflow.json` (or `telegram-agent-workflow-v2.json`). 4. Click the chat bubble and start commanding your Kubernetes cluster! --- ## Key Engineering Takeaways 1. **Sub-Second LLMs Transform DevOps UX:** Fast models like Llama 3.3 70B on Groq make agentic multi-tool investigations fast enough for live incident triage. 2. **Granular Tooling Enforces RBAC Boundaries:** Splitting `kubectl` into 20 discrete tools rather than giving the agent raw bash access enables fine-grained permission control and safety confirmations. 3. **Bridge Desktop and Mobile Operations:** Combining web chat with Telegram and Cloudflare Tunnels gives SREs full operational visibility whether at their desk or on call. Inspect the complete repository, workflow definitions, and Dockerfiles on GitHub: [gitanshulbisht/AI-Kubernetes-Agent-Teamate](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Kubernetes-Agent-Teamate).

# Automating Cloud FinOps: Building an AI Cloud Cost Detective with FastAPI, React 19, and NVIDIA NIM **Author:** [Anshul Bisht](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht) **Date:** June 2026 **Category:** Cloud FinOps / Full-Stack Engineering / AI Systems **Reading Time:** 12 min **Repository:** [github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Cloud-Cost-Detective](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Cloud-Cost-Detective) --- ## Executive Summary Cloud waste is an expensive, silent epidemic. Engineering organizations routinely spend 20% to 35% more on cloud infrastructure than necessary, driven by abandoned development environments, oversized virtual machine tiers, unattached storage disks, and idle load balancers. While cloud providers offer native tools like Azure Advisor or AWS Cost Explorer, these tools rely on rigid, one-size-fits-all metric thresholds and produce generic recommendations that require substantial manual effort to translate into remediation scripts. **AI Cloud Cost Detective** is a production-ready, full-stack FinOps platform that automates the entire cloud cost investigation lifecycle. Built on **FastAPI (Python 3.12+)**, **React 19 + TypeScript**, **PostgreSQL 15**, and **NVIDIA NIM** (Meta Llama 3.3 70B Instruct), the application scans Azure Resource Groups, streams real-time analysis progress to the browser over **WebSockets**, and delivers context-aware cost diagnoses with ready-to-run **Azure CLI remediation commands**. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Client["Frontend Client (React 19 + Vite 8)"] UI["Tailwind CSS v4 Dashboard"] LiveStream["WebSocket Progress HUD"] HistoryView["Historical Analyses & Reports"] end subgraph Backend["FastAPI Asynchronous Engine"] AuthRouter["Auth Router (JWT + Bcrypt)"] AnalysisRouter["Analysis Router & Orchestrator"] WSHandler["WebSocket Stream Manager"] Scanner["Azure Resource Scanner
(azure-mgmt-resource / Mock Fallback)"] end subgraph External["External Services & AI"] AzureAPI["Azure Resource Management REST API"] NIM["NVIDIA NIM Inference Engine
meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct
integrate.api.nvidia.com"] end subgraph Storage["Persistence Tier (PostgreSQL 15)"] DB[("aicloudcost-pg
• users (Bcrypt Hashes)
• analyses (JSONB Reports & Savings)")] end UI -->|HTTP /api/analyze| AnalysisRouter LiveStream <-->|ws:// /ws/progress/{id}| WSHandler AnalysisRouter --> Scanner --> AzureAPI AnalysisRouter --> NIM AnalysisRouter --> DB WSHandler -.-> LiveStream ``` --- ## The FinOps Dilemma: Why Native Cloud Tools Fall Short Platform and FinOps teams face common frustrations with traditional cloud provider advisory tools: 1. **Lack of Contextual Understanding:** Native tools look at fixed metrics in isolation. If a backup VM has 2% average CPU utilization, Azure Advisor flags it as an idle waste. An LLM, however, can inspect resource tags (e.g., `environment: disaster-recovery`, `tier: standby`), understand *why* the VM exists, and avoid recommending dangerous deallocations. 2. **Generic Advice vs. Actionable Fixes:** Native tools advise: *"Consider resizing this virtual machine."* But what tier should it become? What is the command? AI Cloud Cost Detective outputs the exact, copy-pasteable `az vm resize --resource-group prod-rg --name api-vm --size Standard_B2s` command. 3. **Multi-Cloud Extensibility:** Native tools lock you into a single console. By abstracting the resource scanner from the AI reasoning engine, this architecture can be adapted to AWS, GCP, or on-premises Kubernetes by swapping the ingestion client. --- ## Architectural Deep Dive ### 1. The Asynchronous Backend (FastAPI + asyncpg) The backend is built around Python's asynchronous event loop: - **FastAPI with asyncpg:** Employs raw SQL queries and connection pooling via `asyncpg` for high-concurrency database access without ORM overhead. - **Background Tasks & WebSocket Broadcasting:** When an analysis is requested via `POST /api/analyze`, the API server returns an analysis ID immediately and dispatches an asynchronous background task. Progress updates (`scanning_azure`, `evaluating_costs`, `formatting_recommendations`, `complete`) are broadcast in real time to the client's WebSocket connection (`/ws/progress/{id}`). ### 2. Dual-Mode Azure Scanner (Live API + Mock Mode) Cloud SDKs often require extensive subscription permissions and live cloud credentials. To ensure rapid local development and automated CI testing, the scanner implements an automatic fallback: ```python class AzureScanner: def __init__(self): self.live_mode = bool(os.getenv("AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID") and os.getenv("AZURE_CLIENT_ID")) async def scan_resource_group(self, resource_group: str) -> list[dict]: if self.live_mode: return await self._scan_live_azure(resource_group) else: logger.info("Live Azure credentials missing; falling back to mock resource generator") return self._load_mock_resources(resource_group) ``` - **Live Mode:** Connects to Azure Resource Manager using `azure-identity` (Client Secret / DefaultAzureCredential) and queries all deployed resources, SKUs, and tags in the target resource group. - **Mock Mode:** Generates a realistic mock resource group populated with unattached managed disks, over-provisioned Standard_D8s_v5 VMs, and unassociated Public IPs. --- ## The AI Intelligence Layer: NVIDIA NIM Llama 3.3 70B The resource inventory is compiled into a structured JSON payload and dispatched to **NVIDIA NIM** (`integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1`) running `meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct`. ### The Structured FinOps System Prompt The prompt enforces structured analytical reasoning: - **Analyze Provisioning:** Evaluate VM sizes against stated resource group purposes. - **Identify Zombie Assets:** Detect unattached OS and data disks, idle load balancers, and unused Public IPs. - **Project Quantifiable Savings:** Estimate monthly dollar cost reductions based on current Azure retail pricing benchmarks. - **Generate Remediation Commands:** Formulate exact `az` CLI commands for every identified issue. ### JSON Schema Output Specification The model returns a strict JSON object validated via Pydantic: ```json { "summary": { "resources_scanned": 14, "issues_detected": 4, "estimated_monthly_savings_usd": 348.50, "health_score": 68 }, "issues": [ { "severity": "CRITICAL", "resource_name": "data-disk-abandoned-01", "resource_type": "Microsoft.Compute/disks", "issue_type": "UNATTACHED_DISK", "reason": "Managed disk of size 512GB (Premium SSD) has no active VM attachment. Incurring silent storage charges.", "estimated_monthly_waste_usd": 76.80, "remediation_command": "az disk delete --resource-group dev-sandbox --name data-disk-abandoned-01 --yes" }, { "severity": "HIGH", "resource_name": "dev-api-vm", "resource_type": "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines", "issue_type": "OVERPROVISIONED", "reason": "Virtual machine is running Standard_D8s_v5 ($280/mo) in a sandbox environment tagged 'test-env'. Can be resized to Standard_B2s.", "estimated_monthly_waste_usd": 235.00, "remediation_command": "az vm resize --resource-group dev-sandbox --name dev-api-vm --size Standard_B2s" } ] } ``` --- ## Frontend Architecture: React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS v4 The frontend delivers a modern single-page application built on **Vite 8** and **Tailwind CSS v4**: - **Real-Time Progress Stepper:** An interactive WebSocket listener dynamically updates a progress stepper as the backend moves through discovery and AI reasoning phases. - **Interactive Remediation Terminal:** Each identified cost issue includes a copyable terminal card containing the generated Azure CLI command, allowing SREs to apply fixes instantly. - **Historical Analysis Browser:** Analyses are persisted in PostgreSQL (`JSONB`), allowing teams to revisit previous audit runs, compare historical savings curves, and export compliance reports. --- ## Database Architecture (PostgreSQL 15) The database schema is streamlined and optimized for JSON document persistence: ```sql CREATE TABLE users ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL, password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() ); CREATE TABLE analyses ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, resource_group VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL, resources_scanned INTEGER NOT NULL, issues_found INTEGER NOT NULL, estimated_savings NUMERIC(10, 2) NOT NULL, analysis_result JSONB NOT NULL, status VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() ); ``` Using PostgreSQL's `JSONB` type allows arbitrary metadata and model revisions to be preserved without requiring continuous database schema migrations. --- ## Hands-On: Setting Up AI Cloud Cost Detective ### 1. Clone & Provision Database ```bash git clone https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Cloud-Cost-Detective.git cd AI-Cloud-Cost-Detective # Launch PostgreSQL 15 container docker run --name aicloudcost-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -e POSTGRES_DB=aicloudcost -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:15 ``` ### 2. Configure Backend ```bash cd backend python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # Configure DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, and NVIDIA_API_KEY # (Leave Azure credentials blank to automatically use Mock Mode) uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 ``` ### 3. Launch Frontend ```bash cd ../frontend npm install npm run dev ``` Open `http://localhost:5173` to launch the application. --- ## Key Engineering Takeaways 1. **Context-Aware LLMs Transform FinOps:** By analyzing naming conventions, tag metadata, and resource relationships, LLMs eliminate the false positives that plague traditional threshold-based cost tools. 2. **Actionability Is the Ultimate Metric:** Providing an exact CLI remediation command turns passive reporting into instant, high-impact cloud cost savings. 3. **WebSockets Prevent UI Freezes During Deep AI Invocations:** Multi-step LLM reasoning can take 5–15 seconds. Real-time streaming status updates keep operators engaged and informed. Inspect the complete source code, database migrations, and frontend components on GitHub: [gitanshulbisht/AI-Cloud-Cost-Detective](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AI-Cloud-Cost-Detective).

# AI Kubernetes Agent: Automated Root Cause Analysis, Severity Scoring, and Suggested Fixes with Next.js & Gemini 2.5 Pro **Author:** [Anshul Bisht](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht) **Date:** June 2026 **Category:** Kubernetes / Site Reliability Engineering / Next.js & AI **Reading Time:** 9 min **Repository:** [github.com/gitanshulbisht/AIKubernetsAgent](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AIKubernetsAgent) --- ## Executive Summary When a Kubernetes microservice begins degraded operations, the immediate operational bottleneck is rarely the complexity of the fix itself. The real bottleneck is **time to diagnosis (MTTD)**: collecting scattered logs, cross-referencing warning events, auditing resource quotas, and deciphering cryptic failure modes like `CrashLoopBackOff` or `ErrImagePull`. **AI Kubernetes Agent** is an end-to-end full-stack troubleshooting platform designed to automate the initial investigation of Kubernetes incidents. Built on **Next.js**, **Tailwind CSS with glassmorphism**, **FastAPI**, and **Google Gemini 2.5 Pro** via OpenRouter, with real-time state synchronization via **InsForge (PostgreSQL)**, the agent collects multi-tier cluster evidence with a single click and synthesizes actionable **Root Cause Analyses (RCA)**, confidence scores, and ready-to-run `kubectl` remediation commands. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Frontend["Next.js Glassmorphism UI (port 3000)"] Dashboard["Operator Dashboard
(One-Click 'Investigate Cluster')"] AuditView["Historical RCA Audit Log"] LiveFeed["Real-Time Subscription Socket"] end subgraph Orchestrator["FastAPI Backend (port 8002)"] API["FastAPI Orchestrator"] K8sCollector["Evidence Collection Subsystem
(kubectl subprocess wrappers & Loguru)"] end subgraph Cluster["Kubernetes Infrastructure (kind)"] K8sAPI["Kubernetes API Server"] Workloads["Pods · Deployments · Services · Events"] end subgraph AI["AI Reasoning Engine"] OpenRouter["OpenRouter API Gateway"] Gemini["Google Gemini 2.5 Pro
Deep Systems Reasoning"] end subgraph Persistence["InsForge Cloud Platform"] DB[("PostgreSQL Database
• diagnoses (JSONB)
• real-time subscriptions")] end Dashboard -->|Trigger Investigation| API API --> K8sCollector -->|Query State| K8sAPI <--> Workloads K8sCollector -->|Consolidated Evidence Payload| OpenRouter --> Gemini Gemini -->|Structured Diagnosis JSON| API API -->|Persist RCA Record| DB DB -.->|Socket Push| LiveFeed --> Dashboard AuditView <--> DB ``` --- ## The Problem: The Cognitive Fatigue of Kubernetes Incident Triage Every DevOps engineer and SRE recognizes the ritual of manual Kubernetes debugging: 1. `kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running` 2. `kubectl describe pod -n ` 3. `kubectl logs -n --previous` 4. `kubectl get events -n --sort-by='.metadata.creationTimestamp'` 5. `kubectl get svc,endpoints -n ` When incidents strike under pressure, engineers must assemble these disconnected pieces into a coherent hypothesis. Junior engineers struggle to distinguish between transient warnings and catastrophic configuration errors, while senior engineers spend hours performing routine triage that could easily be automated. AI Kubernetes Agent automates this multi-step investigative runbook end-to-end. --- ## High-Level Architecture & Component Roles The application consists of three decoupled layers: ### 1. Modern Next.js Frontend - **Glassmorphism UI:** Built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, featuring frosted-glass panels, clean metric dials, and high-contrast terminal code snippets. - **One-Click Investigation:** Operators trigger cluster-wide or namespace-specific evaluations with a single click. - **Audit & History Log:** Past diagnostic reports are preserved, enabling platform teams to review incident trends over time. ### 2. FastAPI Evidence Collector - **Asynchronous Python Core:** Utilizes `FastAPI` and `httpx` for high-throughput request orchestration. - **Subprocess Wrappers:** Executes targeted, non-destructive `kubectl` queries to capture active pod states, exit codes, recent log tails, and namespace event queues. - **Payload Synthesis:** Cleans and strips redundant cluster noise, assembling a structured evidence payload for LLM consumption. ### 3. Reasoning Layer (Google Gemini 2.5 Pro) - **Deep Systems Reasoning:** Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro excels at long-context comprehension and structural reasoning. It evaluates complex multi-container pod interactions and configuration discrepancies that trip up smaller models. - **Structured JSON Schema:** The model produces a strictly typed diagnosis object detailing the core problem, root cause explanation, confidence percentage, and verified command-line fixes. --- ## Deep Dive: The Evidence Collection & Synthesis Pipeline When an investigation is initiated: ``` [ Operator Clicks "Investigate Cluster" ] │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Evidence Collection Layer (FastAPI) │ │ 1. Scan all pods in non-Ready states │ │ 2. Extract last 100 log lines per container │ │ 3. Pull warning events from event queue │ │ 4. Check Deployment & Service status │ └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Prompt Engineering & Context Assembly │ │ • Format cluster state into clean JSON │ │ • Inject Senior SRE Persona Guidelines │ └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Gemini 2.5 Pro Structured Synthesis │ │ • Root Cause Analysis (RCA) │ │ • Technical Breakdown │ │ • Confidence Score (0–100%) │ │ • Copyable kubectl Fix Commands │ └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘ │ ▼ [ Stream Results via InsForge to Dashboard ] ``` ### The Structured Diagnostic Contract The model emits structured JSON adhering to the following schema: ```json { "incident_title": "Database Connection Pool Exhaustion in Payment Service", "affected_resources": [ { "kind": "Pod", "name": "payment-service-84f6974db9-2kx4w", "namespace": "production", "state": "CrashLoopBackOff" } ], "root_cause_analysis": "The payment-service pod is exiting with code 1 due to an unhandled PostgreSQL connection pool timeout. Pod logs show 'Fatal: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections'. Recent events indicate a sudden traffic spike with insufficient replica scaling.", "confidence_score": 94, "severity": "CRITICAL", "suggested_fix": { "explanation": "Scale out the database proxy connection pool limit and temporarily throttle non-critical background jobs.", "commands": [ "kubectl patch configmap db-config -n production --type merge -p '{\"data\":{\"max_connections\":\"250\"}}'", "kubectl rollout restart deployment/payment-service -n production" ] } } ``` --- ## Local Hands-On Walkthrough ### 1. Provision Local Cluster with Test Chaos Scenarios The repository includes pre-built chaos scenarios (`test-scenarios.yaml`) that simulate common failure modes: ```bash # Create local kind cluster kind create cluster --name kubernetes-demo-cluster # Deploy test failure workloads (CrashLoop, Bad Image, OOM) kubectl apply -f test-scenarios.yaml ``` ### 2. Configure & Start FastAPI Backend ```bash python3 -m venv backend/venv source backend/venv/bin/activate pip install -r backend/requirements.txt # Create backend/.env cat < backend/.env OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your_openrouter_key OPENROUTER_MODEL=google/gemini-2.5-pro INSFORGE_URL=your_insforge_url INSFORGE_ANON_KEY=your_insforge_anon_key EOF # Launch server on port 8002 export PYTHONPATH=. uvicorn backend.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8002 --reload ``` ### 3. Launch Next.js Frontend ```bash cd frontend npm install # Create frontend/.env.local cat < .env.local NEXT_PUBLIC_INSFORGE_URL=your_insforge_url NEXT_PUBLIC_INSFORGE_ANON_KEY=your_insforge_anon_key EOF npm run dev ``` Open `http://localhost:3000`, connect your local `kind` context, and click **Investigate Cluster**. In seconds, the dashboard will display a complete breakdown of every broken workload with ready-to-run fixes. --- ## Key Engineering Takeaways 1. **Automating Evidence Collection Reduces MTTD by 80%:** The most tedious part of incident response is data gathering. Running automated diagnostic collectors eliminates human latency. 2. **Confidence Scores Build Trust:** Providing a calibrated confidence metric (e.g., 94% vs. 60%) helps operators determine whether to apply a fix automatically or investigate further. 3. **Structured Schemas Enable Automation:** Emitting typed JSON rather than free-form conversational text allows downstream workflows to execute fixes or integrate into CI/CD pipelines programmatically. Inspect the complete codebase, Next.js components, and test scenarios on GitHub: [gitanshulbisht/AIKubernetsAgent](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/AIKubernetsAgent).

# Building a Production-Grade Cloud Platform: AWS EKS, Terraform, GitOps with ArgoCD, and OpenTelemetry Full-Stack Observability **Author:** [Anshul Bisht](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht) **Date:** May 2026 **Category:** Cloud Platform Engineering / AWS / GitOps & SRE **Reading Time:** 13 min **Repository:** [github.com/gitanshulbisht/ProductionGradeEndToEndDevOps](https://github.com/gitanshulbisht/ProductionGradeEndToEndDevOps) --- ## Executive Summary Building a modern enterprise cloud platform requires far more than spinning up a Kubernetes cluster with a few shell scripts. True production readiness demands a strict **separation of concerns**, declarative **Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC)**, continuous reconciliation via **GitOps**, fine-grained IAM authentication via **IRSA**, and **distributed observability** across every layer of the microservices fleet. **Production-Grade End-to-End DevOps** is a comprehensive, production-hardened platform repository. Platform infrastructure (Terraform VPCs, EKS node groups, IAM policies) changes deliberately and slowly. Decoupling them ensures a developer pushing a typo in application logic cannot trigger massive Terraform state recalculations. 2. **Blast Radius & Least Privilege:** Application developers have merge permissions in application repositories. However, they are restricted from altering AWS VPC route tables, tearing down EKS clusters, or elevating IAM permissions in the Platform repo. 3. **The GitOps Contract:** When application CI pipelines build a new container image, they do not touch the cluster directly. Instead, CI opens an automated Pull Request in this Platform repository to update the image tag in the application manifest. Argo CD detects the git commit and safely deploys it to the cluster. --- ## Architectural Pillar 2: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform) The underlying cloud infrastructure is codified using official HashiCorp AWS modules to guarantee reproducibility, modularity, and security: ### 1. VPC Architecture & Cost Optimization - Spans two Availability Zones (`us-east-1a`, `us-east-1b`) for high availability. - Features isolated Public and Private subnets. EKS worker nodes run exclusively in private subnets, completely shielded from direct public internet ingress. - **Cost Engineering:** Utilizes a single NAT Gateway across both AZs for non-production environments, reducing AWS fixed infrastructure bills by ~$32/month while maintaining full outbound connectivity for container image pulls. ### 2. EKS Cluster Configuration (v1.30) - Configured with managed node groups utilizing `t3.large` instances (2 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM) to handle memory-intensive tracing collectors and distributed observability pipelines. - Implements **IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA)**: Rather than granting broad AWS permissions to entire worker nodes, pods bind to fine-grained IAM roles via OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity federation. ```bash # Provisioning the entire AWS foundation cd terraform terraform init terraform apply -auto-approve # Update local kubeconfig to connect to EKS aws eks update-kubeconfig --region us-east-1 --name otel-demo-cluster ``` --- ## Architectural Pillar 3: Declarative GitOps with Argo CD Deployments are governed entirely by Argo CD following declarative GitOps principles. ### Overcoming the Large CRD Problem via Server-Side Apply Argo CD introduces extensive Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). Standard `kubectl apply` commands store the previous state inside the `kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration` annotation. Because this annotation has a hard 256KB limit, standard apply commands fail on large CRDs. The deployment overcomes this by enforcing **Kubernetes Server-Side Apply (SSA)**: ```bash kubectl create namespace argocd kubectl apply --server-side=true --force-conflicts -k gitops/1-argocd-init ``` Server-Side Apply calculates and reconciles state directly on the API server, bypassing annotation size constraints entirely. ### Self-Healing & Automated Pruning Argo CD applications are configured with automated sync policies: ```yaml syncPolicy: automated: prune: true selfHeal: true syncOptions: - CreateNamespace=true ``` If an operator manually deletes a pod or modifies a service in the cluster via `kubectl`, Argo CD immediately flags the discrepancy and restores the cluster to the exact state committed in Git. --- ## Architectural Pillar 4: The OpenTelemetry Observability Fleet To validate the platform under enterprise-scale conditions, the cluster runs the **OpenTelemetry Astronomy Shop Demo**—a fleet of 25+ distributed microservices implemented across 10 programming languages (Go, Java, C#, Python, Rust, Node.js, PHP, Erlang, Ruby, C++). ``` [ Frontend Proxy ] ──▶ [ Checkout Service (Go) ] ──▶ [ Payment Service (Node) ] │ │ ▼ ▼ [ Shipping (Rust) ] [ Currency (C++) ] │ │ └──────────────┬────────────────┘ ▼ [ OpenTelemetry Collector ] ┌────────┴────────┐ ▼ ▼ [ Jaeger Distributed ] [ Prometheus & ] [ Tracing UI ] [ Grafana RED ] ``` ### 1. Jaeger Distributed Tracing Every HTTP and gRPC request carries W3C Trace Context headers. Engineers can view distributed request traces across all 25+ microservices in the Jaeger UI, pinpointing millisecond-level bottlenecks and network latency spikes. ### 2. Grafana RED Metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) Pre-configured Grafana dashboards visualize real-time request rates, error percentages, and latency percentiles (P50, P90, P99) across individual microservices, augmented by exemplars linking metric spikes directly to Jaeger traces. --- ## Layer 7 Ingress: Migrating to the AWS Load Balancer Controller Standard Kubernetes services of type `LoadBalancer` create legacy AWS Classic Load Balancers (CLBs), which incur high per-service costs and lack advanced path-based routing. To modernize ingress: 1. **IRSA Provisioning:** Terraform provisions an IAM role granting permissions to manage AWS Application Load Balancers and associates it with the `aws-load-balancer-controller` Kubernetes ServiceAccount. 2. **GitOps Deployment:** Argo CD deploys the AWS Load Balancer Controller into `kube-system`. 3. **Ingress Resource:** The platform replaces the legacy ELB with an Ingress resource managed by the controller: ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: Ingress metadata: name: otel-demo-ingress namespace: otel-demo annotations: kubernetes.io/ingress.class: alb alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip spec: rules: - http: paths: - path: / pathType: Prefix backend: service: name: frontend-proxy port: number: 8080 ``` ### Real-World Debugging: Strict Helm Schemas During the ingress migration, deploying the OpenTelemetry v2.2.0 Helm chart failed due to a strict JSON Schema validation failure: the chart maintainers had changed the configuration key from `frontendProxy` to `frontend-proxy`. Because Argo CD manages state transactionally, the deployment failed gracefully without disturbing the existing active workloads. Once the manifest was corrected in Git, Argo CD automatically synced and provisioned the modern AWS Application Load Balancer. --- ## Continuous Integration: GitHub Actions Quality Gates Every pull request triggers an automated GitHub Actions CI pipeline (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): - **Terraform Formatting & Validation:** Executes `terraform fmt -check` and `terraform validate` to enforce clean IaC patterns. - **YAML Linting:** Scans all Kubernetes and Argo CD manifests using `yamllint` to catch syntax errors before commits reach the `main` branch. --- ## Graceful Cluster Teardown Procedure Because the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions external cloud resources (ALBs, Target Groups, Security Groups) dynamically inside AWS, running a naive `terraform destroy` will fail if the ALB still has active dependencies. To prevent orphaned AWS resources and billing leaks: ```bash # 1. Delete the GitOps applications first (allows controller to de-provision ALBs) kubectl delete -f gitops/2-apps/opentelemetry-demo.yaml kubectl delete -f gitops/2-apps/aws-lbc.yaml # Wait 3 minutes for AWS Application Load Balancer to delete in the AWS Console # 2. Destroy the underlying Terraform infrastructure cd terraform terraform destroy -auto-approve ``` --- ## Key Engineering Takeaways 1. **Codify Separation of Concerns Early:** Keeping platform code strictly decoupled from application code prevents operational cross-contamination and simplifies security auditing. 2. **Server-Side Apply Is Essential for Modern Operators:** Large CRDs like Argo CD and OpenTelemetry Collector exceed annotation limits; adopting Server-Side Apply from day one prevents rollout blockers. 3. **Observability Must Be Full-Stack:** Distributed tracing (Jaeger) and metrics (Prometheus/Grafana) are not optional add-ons; they are required infrastructure for operating microservices reliably in production.
